turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, what brings me in is... I just cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. I work at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street, you know, the one right next to that little Italian bakery? Oh, they make these incredible almond biscotti there. I try not to go in every morning, but the smell just gets you right when you're unlocking the front door of the shop. 

But anyway, at work, I've got tickets, receipts, workshop notes, and customer jobs all piled together in these huge stacks on the counter. It's gotten so bad I just stare at it and I do not know what to handle first. Just yesterday, Mrs. Gable came in looking for her husband's wool coat, and I was digging through this mountain of paper trying to find her ticket... wool is so heavy, you know? My grandmother used to knit these thick wool sweaters that would just itch like crazy. I could never wear them, no matter how cold it got outside... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, just the piles at work. It's really becoming a problem.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot keep their work in order, with items piled up and an inability to know what to handle first.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets easily distracted by unrelated thoughts (the bakery, grandmother's wool sweaters) and loses their train of thought during the conversation.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always struggled with this kind of disorganization and difficulty staying on task, or is this something that has only started bothering you more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I think I've always been a little all over the place, but it hasn't always been this much of a disaster. It's really been causing real trouble for about... oh, I'd say two years and two months now. That's exactly when I started changing the business into this more complicated boutique model. 

We started taking in all these delicate, high-end pieces, you know? Like vintage lace and silk. Silk is just beautiful, isn't it? Though it's a complete nightmare if you spill something on it. My sister actually had this gorgeous silk dress for her rehearsal dinner years ago, and she spilled a whole glass of merlot right down the front. We tried everything—club soda, salt, you name it. She was so upset she almost called off the wedding! Which, honestly, might have been for the best because her husband turned out to be a real piece of work. He ended up moving to Florida and buying a boat, if you can believe that. Who just buys a boat and leaves? 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh! Yes, the boutique model at the shop. Since we switched to that about two years and a couple months ago, the special instructions and all the extra tags are just... I can't keep it straight anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states she cannot keep straight the special instructions and extra tags, indicating difficulty with details.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient admits she has 'always been a little all over the place' and is currently struggling to manage the more complicated boutique model.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by her own unrelated thoughts, going off on a tangent about silk and her sister's wedding.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from her business model to a story about her sister's ex-husband buying a boat, completely losing her original train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, did you struggle with staying focused or staying organized back then as well?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask about school. I remember my mother used to get so frustrated. Even back in grade school, my teachers would always tell her that I was bright, but just... scattered. Always talking out of turn, losing my papers, needing constant reminders to finish my work. 

My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins, she was this tiny woman who always wore these huge, colorful scarves. I mean, they were practically blankets! She had this one that was bright orange and turquoise, and I used to just stare at it during math class. Math was always so boring anyway. Fractions? Who really needs to know how to multiply fractions in the real world unless you're baking? And I do love to bake. I make a mean banana bread. The trick is you have to let the bananas get almost completely black on the counter before you mash them. Most people throw them out when they look like that, but that's when they have the most sugar! My neighbor, Gary, he always asks me to make him a loaf around the holidays. Gary's a nice guy, but he lets his dog bark at all hours of the night. A little terrier mix, I think. Just yip, yip, yip... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I was always losing my homework and talking when I shouldn't have been. My mother was always getting called in for parent-teacher conferences.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states they needed constant reminders to finish their work in school.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms the doctor's question about struggling to stay organized by describing themselves as having been 'scattered'.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly recalls 'losing my papers' and 'losing my homework' during grade school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (a teacher's scarf) and demonstrates distractibility during the response by going on a tangent and forgetting the question.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in school, did you often feel like you had a motor running inside you, or did you find it difficult to stay seated when you were expected to?
turns.patient_response:
Well, staying seated... yes, that's always been a thing, even now. Like, I'm on this church committee, and we have these meetings, or even when I have to go to those fabric-care trainings for work. I just cannot sit still the whole time like everybody else does. I'm always finding some reason to get up—like, oh, I need to grab some water, or I need to check on some papers, or whatever. 

Speaking of water, the water pressure at my house has been just terrible lately. I called a plumber, this guy named Sal, and he said it's because the pipes in my neighborhood are practically ancient. They were put in back in the 1950s, I think. Sal was telling me all about galvanized steel versus copper, and honestly, it's fascinating how much goes into just getting water out of a tap. He said he could replace the main line, but it would cost a fortune. And with the shop being so chaotic right now, I just don't have the time to deal with a whole plumbing disaster. My backyard would be completely dug up, and my rose bushes... I have these beautiful hybrid tea roses that took me years to get right. If they get dug up, I don't know what I'd do. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, feeling like a motor's running and not staying in my seat. Yeah, I definitely still do that. I just have to keep moving.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by her own unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about plumbing and roses before forgetting the initial question.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms she cannot sit still during meetings and trainings, always finding reasons to get up when expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly agrees with the doctor's description of feeling like a motor is running, stating she just has to keep moving.

turns.doctor_question: In your daily life, do you often find yourself acting or speaking without thinking, such as interrupting others during conversations or making impulsive decisions that you later regret?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, all the time. I really do. At the shop, I'll just cut right into my staff's conversations, or I'll just reach right over and fix how they're sorting the clothes before they even ask me for help. I know it comes off like I'm butting in, but I just do it without thinking. 

Like the other day, Brenda—she's one of my girls up front—she was sorting this big pile of winter coats. And winter coats are so bulky, you know? My grandmother used to have this stunning heavy wool peacoat she wore for literally thirty years. Thirty years! They just don't make clothes like that anymore. Everything now is that fast fashion stuff, all cheap synthetic blends that fall apart after a couple of washes. I was at the mall last weekend trying to find a simple cotton blouse, just a plain white button-down, and everything was polyester. Polyester makes me sweat just looking at it. Plus it holds onto odors terribly, which I know all about from the dry cleaning business. And the prices! They want sixty dollars for something that's going to pill in a month. I got so frustrated I just gave up and went to the food court and bought a pretzel instead. The cinnamon sugar kind, they're so good when they're warm... 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, interrupting. Yes. I just jump right in and take over the sorting from Brenda, or I'll blurt something out right over someone else talking. I don't mean to be rude, it just completely slips out before my brain can catch it.

symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly admits to cutting into staff conversations, taking over their tasks unasked, and blurting things out over others talking.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from sorting coats to her grandmother's coat, fast fashion, polyester, and pretzels, before losing her train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in elementary school, did you frequently find yourself unable to stay in your seat or blurting out answers before the teacher finished asking the question?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, even back then I suppose I did. But it's not just a childhood thing, really. It happens to me all the time now. I'll just jump right in with an answer before someone even finishes asking me something. Like with my daughter, or a customer at the shop, or even that trainer at the fabric-care seminar I mentioned. I just blurt it out. And half the time, I realize I answered the completely wrong thing because I didn't wait to hear the whole question. 

My daughter, she gets so annoyed with me. She's 28 now, living in Chicago, working in marketing. Or is it public relations? I can never keep those two straight. It's all just sitting at a computer all day anyway. I tell her she needs to get up and stretch more, maybe get one of those standing desks. I saw this special on the morning news about how sitting is the new smoking. Can you believe that? They had this whole segment with a doctor showing how it affects your spine and your circulation. It made me so glad I'm on my feet all day at the dry cleaners, even if my arches ache by five o'clock. I bought these orthotic inserts from the pharmacy, the ones where you stand on the machine and it maps your foot? They cost a pretty penny, but let me tell you, they really do help. Though you have to make sure you put them in the right shoes. I tried putting them in my favorite loafers, but it made them too tight across the top, right over the instep...

Oh, I'm sorry, I'm wandering again, aren't I? What were you asking? Oh, blurting things out. Yes, I do that a lot. I just jump the gun and answer before people are done talking, and then I end up looking foolish because I answered the wrong thing.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient agrees with the doctor's question about having trouble staying in her seat during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states she frequently blurts out answers before people finish asking their questions, both in the past and currently.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over the last six months, would you say that you have been struggling significantly with both the disorganization and trouble staying on task, as well as the constant need to move and blurting things out, or has one of those types of problems been much more dominant than the other?
turns.patient_response:
Well, honestly, I think it's both. It's really both of them happening all the time. I'm always misplacing things at the shop, getting distracted, leaving tickets half-written... and at the same time, I can't sit still and I'm always talking over people. 

Speaking of tickets, we had to switch to this new computer system last month because the old register finally died. It just completely gave out on a Tuesday afternoon. The screen went completely black, and the receipt printer made this horrible grinding noise. I had to call the tech support line, and I was on hold for forty-five minutes. Forty-five minutes! And they just play that same looping elevator music over and over. It gets stuck in your head for days. I was humming it while making dinner that night. I made meatloaf, my mother's recipe, with the brown sugar glaze on top. But I forgot to buy breadcrumbs, so I had to crush up some Ritz crackers instead. Honestly, I think it turned out better with the crackers. It gave it a nice buttery flavor. My husband said it was the best meatloaf I've made in years, though he always puts too much ketchup on it anyway, so I'm not sure his palate is all that refined. He buys that fancy organic ketchup now, the one in the glass bottle, but it's so hard to get it out. You have to smack the bottom of it, and then it all comes rushing out at once and ruins the plate...

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, which one is worse. Yeah, no, it's definitely both. The disorganization and the blurting and moving around... they're both just as bad as each other. They really are.

symptom_reasoning.S004: Patient mentions leaving tickets half-written at work, indicating a failure to finish workplace duties.
symptom_reasoning.S005: Patient explicitly confirms struggling with disorganization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: Patient states they are always misplacing things at the shop.
symptom_reasoning.S008: Patient explicitly notes getting distracted and demonstrates this by losing their train of thought during the response.
symptom_reasoning.S012: Patient describes an inability to sit still and a constant need for moving around.
symptom_reasoning.S015: Patient demonstrates excessive talking by going on a long, detailed tangent about a broken register, elevator music, and making meatloaf.
symptom_reasoning.S016: Patient confirms that blurting things out is a significant and ongoing problem.
symptom_reasoning.S018: Patient admits to always talking over people, which indicates interrupting or intruding on others' conversations.
